segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Finally, my brothers and sisters, rejoice in the Lord. To write the same things to you is no trouble for me, and for you it is a safeguard.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Watch out for the dogs, watch out for the evil workers, watch out for the mutilation.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God and boast in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: though I myself have grounds for confidence in the flesh as well. If anyone else thinks he can put confidence in the flesh, I can do so more:

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Hebrew born of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as to zeal, a persecutor of the assembly; as to the righteousness that is in the law, proved blameless.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But whatever things were gains to me, these I have come to consider loss because of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: More than that, I consider everything to be loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. Because of him I have suffered the loss of everything, and I consider it dung, so that I may gain Christ

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but the one that comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that rests on faith,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that I may know him and the power of his resurrection and a sharing in his sufferings, being conformed to his death,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: if somehow I may arrive at the resurrection from the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Not that I have already obtained it or have already been made perfect, but I press on in the hope of taking hold of it, because I myself was taken hold of by Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Brothers and sisters, I do not reckon that I myself have taken hold of it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching out toward what lies ahead,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I press on toward the goal, for the prize of God's upward call in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So let all of us who are perfect be of this mind; and if on any point you are of a different mind, God will reveal this to you as well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Only let us keep in step with what we have already reached.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Join together in imitating me, brothers and sisters, and keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For many walk, of whom I have often told you and now tell you even weeping, as enemies of the cross of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Their end is destruction, their god is the belly, and their glory is in their shame; their minds are on earthly things.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For our commonwealth is in the heavens, and from it we eagerly await a savior, the Lord Jesus Christ,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who will transform our lowly body to be conformed to his glorious body, in keeping with the power at work that enables him even to subject all things to himself.

notes.note: The Greek verb was also the ordinary word for both greeting and farewell, so the phrase could mean 'farewell in the Lord', and 'Finally' would then signal a closing. Because joy is a running theme of this letter, most translators take it as 'rejoice', as here.

notes.traditional: the concision; those who mutilate the flesh
notes.note: Paul makes a bitter pun. The Greek word for circumcision is peritomē ('cutting around'), and he calls his opponents the katatomē ('cutting up'), a word related to the Septuagint's term for forbidden pagan gashing of the body. He then claims the title 'the circumcision' for those who worship by God's Spirit. The opponents are generally understood to be teachers urging circumcision on non-Jewish believers.

The Greek word meant a gathering of citizens and, in the Greek Old Testament, Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses 'assembly' throughout.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice. The word covers being in the right, doing what is right, and in verse 9 a right standing that comes from God. Some scholars prefer 'justice' or 'covenant faithfulness' in English.

The word was used in the period both for excrement and for refuse such as table scraps or scrapings thrown out. It was a coarse word in either sense. Most modern versions choose 'rubbish' or 'garbage'; the cruder sense is equally possible and fits the force of Paul's contrast.

The Greek is literally 'faith of Christ', and the grammar allows two readings: the believer's faith in Christ, or Christ's own faithfulness. 'Faith in Christ' is the traditional and still majority reading. 'The faithfulness of Christ' has substantial scholarly support, and on that reading the closing words 'that rests on faith' supply the believer's response.

notes.traditional: that for which (also I was taken hold of by Christ)
notes.note: The Greek connecting phrase can mean 'because' or 'that for which'. On the second reading Paul presses on to take hold of the very thing for which Christ took hold of him. Both readings are well supported, and the difference in overall sense is small.

The adjective means complete, full-grown or perfect, and most modern versions translate it 'mature' here. It is from the same root as the verb in verse 12, where Paul denies that he has 'already been made perfect', and the echo is kept here because it appears deliberate. Many scholars hear some irony: those who are truly 'perfect' know they have not yet arrived.

In the usage of the period the word normally refers to a civic body, a state or a community of citizens, more than to the abstract status of citizenship. 'From it' refers back to this word in the Greek. Philippi was a Roman colony whose citizens were enrolled as citizens of distant Rome, and 'savior' and 'lord' were titles given to the emperor. Many translations use 'citizenship', and some use 'commonwealth' or 'homeland'.
The Greek is plural, reflecting a Hebrew way of speaking about God's dwelling. Most translations flatten it to 'heaven'. This translation keeps the plural wherever the Greek has it.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs in every letter, and translations split between 'brothers', 'brothers and sisters' and 'friends'; it needs a single policy.
The Semitic metaphor for conduct recurs across Paul and John, and translators vary between 'walk', 'live' and 'behave'.
It is rendered 'perfect', 'mature' or 'complete' in different places (Matthew 5:48; 1 Corinthians 2:6; Hebrews 5:14; James 1:4), and the choice affects how readers hear demands for perfection.
Paul's use ranges from the physical body to human nature apart from God, and translations vary between 'flesh', 'sinful nature' and 'human effort'.

candidates.rendering: be of a mind / minds are on
candidates.reason: It is a key verb in Philippians and Romans, rendered 'think', 'set the mind on' or 'have the attitude', and its repetition is thematic and easily lost.
